Abrasive

uh-BRAY-siv -- shares a root with 'erase,' meaning to scrape. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Abrasive is harsh and biting in manner.

New hires often struggled with the head chef's abrasive manner during even the calmest dinner service.

Worked Example

A customer asks a simple question at the return counter, and the clerk snaps back with a sharp, mocking comment that leaves the entire line uncomfortable.

That harsh, wearing-down way of speaking to people is exactly what abrasive describes. Unlike 'blunt,' which is just direct, abrasive actively grates on the people around it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

harsh: Harsh means unpleasantly severe -- a harsh winter, a harsh punishment, a harsh voice. It is a broad word for anything hard to endure. Abrasive is narrower and more personal: a manner of dealing with people that grates on them and wears them down over time.

cutting: A cutting remark wounds in one sharp stroke, like a blade -- brief, targeted, and painful. Abrasive describes something slower and rougher: a whole manner of speaking to people that scrapes at them again and again until they feel worn down.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

gentle: kind and mild in manner

gracious: courteous and pleasant in manner

Where it sits · how much the manner irritates others — brusque → abrasive → grating

brusque vs. abrasive: Brusque is a bit milder than abrasive -- brusque often just means blunt or short with people, while abrasive suggests that manner actively wears on and irritates others over time.

grating vs. abrasive: Grating can feel more persistent than abrasive: abrasive usually describes someone's overall harsh personality, while grating can describe any small, repeated irritation, even something as simple as a habit or sound.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ab-

prefix — ab-: away, off (Latin)

root — -ras-

root — -ras-: to scrape (from Latin radere, past participle rasum)

suffix — -ive

suffix — -ive: tending to; of the nature of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin abradere meant 'to scrape off,' from ab- ('away') and radere ('to scrape'), whose past-participle form rasum gives the -ras- in the middle; -ive turns it into an adjective. Something abrasive wears people down the way scraping wears down a surface -- the same root that gives us erase.

Use the root in a new word: erase

Use the root in a new word: erase: She used the corner of the eraser to carefully erase just one line of the drawing.

Abrasive most often describes a person's harsh personality or manner, as in 'an abrasive management style,' though it can also describe a literally rough, scraping surface.
